newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU states let Renault close car plant - EU's Flynn.
newsitem.headline: EU states let Renault close car plant - EU's Flynn.

text.p: European Union governments were partly to blame for Renault's shock decision to close its car assembly plant in Belgium, European Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn said on Tuesday.

"Member states in 1992 rejected the (European) Commission's proposals regarding tougher sanctions in the event of non compliance by companies (with) the consultation and information procedures with their workers," Flynn told the European Parliament.

The French carmaker's decision to close the profitable Vilvoorde plant, with the loss of 3,100 jobs, had provoked outrage, Flynn said, "because of its abruptness and through its apparent lack of concern with the rights of the employees".
The EU had laws obliging companies to consult fully and inform their workers before taking major decisions but Renault had completely ignored the laws, the Commissioner said.

"Renault management, in a manner which I can only describe as irresponsible, has not complied with its obligations as regards information and consultation of representatives of the workers prior to its decision," he said.

The situation would not have arisen if the member states had accepted the Commission's advice in 1992 and introduced punitive sanctions which would really deter companies tempted to abuse the rules in this way, Flynn said.

"I believe we have now reached the situation where we need to complement the existing Community rules with more general rules which make information and consultation compulsory on a permanent basis in regard to all relevant aspects of the management of companies at national levels," he added.
"The issue of adequate sanctions in the event of non-respect will be a crucial one."

The whole process of European integration could be undermined if the EU did not succeed in finding the right balance "between corporate or economic needs and the social requirements of workers and society as a whole", he said.
